Stems: In free-floating forms, stem is slender, horizontally floating, short, thick and spongy, while in submerged, stem is long, slender, spongy and flexible. c. Leaves: The leaves are generally thin, small and translucent in submerged hydrophytes while large, flat and with waxy coat on entire surface in floating hydrophytes. d. Flowers and reproduction: The flowers are not common in submerged form. They are usually produced on the surface of water or above it. Pollination and dispersal are performed by water, insects and birds. Vegetative reproduction is common. e. Anatomical Adaptation: Aerencyma in submerged leaves and stem is well developed. Mechanical tissue and vascular tissues are poorly developed. The cuticle is absent or poorly developed. Stomata are completely absent in submerged leaves while present on the upper surface of floating forms. f. Physiological adaptation: The aquatic plants exhibit a low compensation point and low osmotic concentration of cell sap. Nutrients are absorbed by the submerged plants through the general plant surface. The gases are exchange from the water though the surface cells (epidermis). Transpiration is absent in submerged hydrophytes however, emergent and free-floating plants have excessive rate of transpiration.

Xerophytes are plants that have adapted to survive in dry or arid environments where water availability is limited. Xerophytes are characteristic plants of desert and semi-desert regions, yet they can grow in mesophytic conditions where water available is in sufficient quantity. Example: Opuntia, Aloe, Begonia, Agave, etc.
According to their adaptations to arid or dry environments, there are three categories of xerophytes:

a. Ephemerals They are xerophytic plants that complete their life cycle in short period of time when sufficient moisture is available. They are also called ‘drought evaders’ or ‘drough escapers’. Since these plants avoid dry seasons. Example: Solanum xanthocarpum, Tephrosia purpurea, etc.

b. Succulent They have specialized tissues for water storage that can store large amounts of water during periods of rainfall or high humidity. In these plants, the succulence, i.e. development of water storing parenchymatous tissues may occur in roots, stems or leaves. The rest of the plant body other than succulent organ is generally reduced. Example: Aloe, Asparagus, Begonia, Agave, etc.

c. True xerophytes or drought resistants The plants which have the ability to maintain growth under critical dry conditions and high temperature are true xerophytes. The plants are woody trees, shrubs or herbs. Example: Acacia nelotica, Nerium, etc.
Adaptation of Xerophytes: The xerophytic plants show following adaptations:
a. Root: They have well developed root system that can penetrate deep into the soil to access moisture. Root hairs are concentrated in abundance near the tips of growing rootlets.

b. Leaves: The leaves, if present, are modified to minimize the rate of transpiration. The modification in leaves may vary from species to species. There are small sized, rolling and folding of leaf blades or delicate leaves which are shed under conditions of less supply of water. The leaves surfaces are generally shining and glazed to reflect light and heat.
c. Stems: The stem of some xerophytes are hard and woody while some plants have succulent type of stem. In some it may modified into thorns.

d. Flower and reproduction: The flower is generally reduced. It generally develop during high moisture availability, such as after rainfall. In some xerophytes the flowers have fleshy structure that can store water. Pollination takes place by wind or gravity. Vegetative propagation is more common.

e. Anatomical adaptation: The leaves have heary cuticular and epidermal layer and waxy coating on its surface to reduce the transpiration. The stomata are sunken type. Conducting and mechanical tissues are well developed.
